moments.title: There are two ways AI progress could go very badly and that we must avoid. First, we could lose control of the future to AI. This is unacceptable; we are unapologetically on Team Humanity, and AI must always serve people
moments.selftext: There are two ways AI progress could go very badly and that we must avoid. First, we could lose control of the future to AI. This is unacceptable; we are unapologetically on Team Humanity, and AI must always serve people. To ensure that, we need ways to ensure that alignment and safety techniques stay ahead of progress in model capabilities. Second, we could end up in a world with too much concentration of power. If an extraordinarily powerful AI is used by one person or company to impress their worldview onto everyone else, the results could be extremely dystopian. Avoiding these two threats requires walking a narrow middle path; for example, one country could gain too much power. Another example is one lab ending up with too much power.

moments.title: The world deserves confidence that American companies developing increasingly capable AI will act responsibly, especially as the trajectory of progress has steepened. Every frontier lab must deliver on this, and there is
moments.selftext: The world deserves confidence that American companies developing increasingly capable AI will act responsibly, especially as the trajectory of progress has steepened. Every frontier lab must deliver on this, and there is no reason any of us should come to work if we cannot. We welcome a federal framework that sets consistent safety requirements for frontier AI. But we do not believe we need to wait for an anti-trust exemption or legislation to begin the work of providing this confidence. Consistent rules to manage frontier risk so that we can maximize the benefits are a good idea (and we are excited by ideas like independent auditors). Years ago, companies like ours developed things like Responsible Scaling Policies and Preparedness Frameworks. Those were good for that moment, and focused primarily on the deployment of completed models, not what happens during their development process. Today's shift to focusing on safe development and evaluation will need new tools. For example, at OpenAI we now formulate explicit safety cases in advance of frontier reinforcement learning runs we expect to significantly increase capability, in addition to the safety work we have long done in advance of model releases. We hope that other companies will learn from our approaches and propose their own; we think shared standards for misalignment, monitoring, and safety will lead to better outcomes. We look forward to collaborating with our colleagues across the industry to formulate the best version of these. When we talk about “pacing”, we do not mean “stopping”. Progress has been rapid and will continue to be. But it should be slower than it otherwise could be; interventions like safety cases and monitoring have significant costs. Pacing will be well worth this cost; no amount of American competitive pressure should justify recklessness, or let capabilities get ahead of alignment and monitoring. Where we will need the help of our government is for international coordination. But first we should do what we can ourselves.

moments.title: A surviving stretch of an ancient Roman road winds through a forest near Klais, Germany. This remarkably well-preserved stretch was part of the Via Raetia, an important Roman road that crossed the Alps and connected nort
moments.selftext: A surviving stretch of an ancient Roman road winds through a forest near Klais, Germany. This remarkably well-preserved stretch was part of the Via Raetia, an important Roman road that crossed the Alps and connected northern Italy with the province of Raetia in what is now southern Germany. Running from the Verona region through the Brenner Pass, Innsbruck, and the Bavarian Alps to Augusta Vindelicorum—modern Augsburg—the route was built or extensively improved around A.D. 200 during the reign of Emperor Septimius Severus. Roman engineers adapted the road to the rugged Alpine terrain by cutting through rock, leveling difficult ground, and strengthening softer sections with stone and gravel. It was designed to carry wheeled traffic transporting soldiers, official messages, food, and commercial goods across the mountains. Deep grooves left by centuries of wagon traffic remain visible near Klais. These ancient wheel ruts offer a striking reminder of the countless travelers and vehicles that once passed through what is now a quiet forest. Roads such as the Via Raetia were essential to Rome’s ability to move armies, officials, information, and goods across vast distances. They also connected distant communities to larger trade networks, helping spread technology, languages, commerce, and Roman culture far beyond Italy. Over time, the Via Raetia became more important than the older Via Claudia Augusta, eventually serving as the principal Roman route across the eastern Alps.
